[b]Mahjong Fundamentals[/b]
Every round, the basic aim is to build a winning hand with the 13 tiles in hand combined with a final 14th tile. This last tile is either drawn yourself or discarded by an opponent player.
Wtih two exceptions (Chiitoitsu and Kokushi Musou), every hand is made up of 4 groups of 3 tiles and a pair of 2. Groups are either runs in a suit of length 3, triplets of identical tiles of size 3, or sets of size 4 (which trigger an additional draw, so that the rest of the hand still completes naturally). An example hand is given below:

column3:
This hand consists of a run of 123-Pin, a run of 234-Sou and of 678-Sou, a pair of 9-Man, and a triplet of Red Dragons, totalling, once more, to 4 groups and a pair.
Critically, this hand meets at least one win condition, more commonly referred to as [i]Yaku[/i]. Here, the hand meets [i]Yakuhai[/i] by having a triplet of Red Dragons. A hand [i]is not valid[/i] if it does not meet at least one Yaku. Refer to the Yaku tab for information on specific Yaku, but Yakuhai is one of the more easily acheivable ones (which have been starred for reference). Riichi is perhaps the most critical to understand, but the explanation behind it is left in the Yaku tab.
A round ends when the number of tiles left in the wall reaches a cutoff. If you have not gone out by this point, you get no points. (There is no ryuukoku tenpai payout by default.)

[b]UltiMahjong Fundamentals[/b]
The whole game is played out across 8 rounds (by default). Every round, your seat wind advances in counterclockwise compass order (N>W>S>E), and every four rounds, the prevalent wind advances in clockwise compass order (E>S>W>N).
At the end of every round, you must have met a minimum score to continue the run. This minimum threshold increases every round. The amount that it will increase next round also increases.
Finishing a round opens the shop, and grants you a static amount of money. You can buy anything you have enough money for, or sell items for money. All unspent money is [i]forfeited[/i] when you close the shop!

[b]UltiMahjong Differences[/b]
A quick list of notable differences between this game and "standard" (were it extant) Riichi:
No furiten.
No shouminkan.
No kuikae restrictions.
The final discarded tile can be called even when not for a win.
Chiitoitsu can contain identical pairs. Daisangen can contain identical triplets. In general, there is no penalty to identicality.
Kazoe does not stack with other yakuman, the other(s) will [i]always[/i] disable it, but it [i]can[/i] stack with itself, e.g. 26 han is a double Kazoe Yakuman. (This has weird scoring implications and may be revisited.)

These are the basic waits formally recognized in Riichi Mahjong. All waits award 2 fu if used as the final wait except Ryanmen, which awards 0. (More complex waits exist, but can be always broken down into a combination of these basic ones, although I leave discovering them as an exercise for the reader.)

column3: Ryanmen: Often translated as "two-sided," this is two adjacent tiles waiting for a third to complete a run from either end.
Shanpon: Two pairs waiting for one to resolve to a triplet.
Penchan and Kanchan: Like Ryanmen, waits on a run to complete, but because of shape or terminality, only waits on one tile instead of two.

Tanki: A single tile waits on a copy of itself to complete a pair. Note the common complex wait pattern Nobetan (e.g. 3456) [i]still counts[/i] as a Tanki wait, even though you are technically waiting on two tiles.

Before we begin, the scoring used here is [i]not the same[/i] as in normal Riichi, although it approximates it fairly closely. (If you already understand Riichi scoring, you should just know: Ron and Tsumo now award the same amount of points, 10 Fu is now worth 400 points exactly instead of ~300, Fu are rounded [i]down[/i] to the nearest 10, and Mangan rounding is smoothed so that more Han always equate to more points earned.)

A hand [i]demands[/i] at least 1 Han and scores 1000 points by default. There are two fundamental factors to inproving this score: Fu and more Han.

Fu are awarded for completing sets and for riskier waits, among other factors. See the "Fu" tab. Every 10 fu rounded [i]down[/i] awards 400 more points.

Han, also known as "doublers," are the more significant factor. All Yaku award some number of Han, and again, you need at least 1. Every additional han doubles the basic score of {1000+fu points}. For example, a 3 Han hand without significant fu is worth {1000×2×2} = 4000 points. A 2 Han hand with 10 fu is worth {1400×2} = 2800 points.
(It may be easier to think of the basic score as {500+200 per 10 Fu}, and the first Han as a doubler as well.)

Once you exceed 8000 points, Fu are no longer counted, and the score rewarded is simply the number of Han multiplied by 2000. After you exceed 10 Han, every additional Han is worth 4000 more points, up to the Yakuman Limit at 13 Han = 32000 points.

Sitting in the East seat multiplies the final value by 1.5. For example, the minimum scoring hand in the East seat is 1500, and a Yakuman is 48000 points.
